title: Part 1, Chapter 4
paragraphs: His mother's letter had tortured him, but on the central issue he had not hesitated for a single moment, even while reading it. The question was settled, irrevocably settled in his mind: "This marriage will never happen while I'm alive, and Mr. Luzhin can go to hell!" "The whole thing is perfectly clear," he muttered to himself with a vicious smile, savoring his resolve. "No, Mother, no, Dunya -- you won't fool me! And they apologize for not asking my advice, for deciding without me! They think it's all arranged and can't be undone -- we'll see about that! A wonderful excuse: 'Pyotr Petrovich is such a busy man that even his wedding has to be rushed, practically by express mail.' No, Dunya, I see through it all. I know what you want to say to me. I know what you were thinking about when you paced all night, and what your prayers were like before the Holy Mother of Kazan in mother's bedroom. The road to Golgotha is bitter.... Hmm... so it's settled then: you've decided to marry a sensible businessman, Avdotya Romanovna, one who has a fortune (_already_ made his fortune -- so much more solid and impressive), a man with two government posts who shares the views of our most progressive generation, as mother writes, and who _seems_ to be kind, as Dunya herself notes. That _seems_ is everything! And that very Dunya is marrying him for that very '_seems_'! Splendid! Splendid!

"...But why did mother write to me about 'our most progressive generation'? Just as a descriptive detail, or to soften me up toward Mr. Luzhin? Oh, how clever of them! And I'd like to know something else: how open were they with each other that day and night and all this time? Was it all spoken aloud, or did they both understand they were thinking the same thing and there was no need to say it, better not to? Probably something like that. From mother's letter it's obvious: he struck her as somewhat rude, and mother in her simplicity shared her observation with Dunya. And of course Dunya was irritated and 'answered angrily.' Naturally! Who wouldn't be, when the point was perfectly clear without any naive questions, and discussing it was useless? And why does she write 'love Dunya, Rodya -- she loves you more than herself'? Is she secretly pricked by guilt over sacrificing her daughter for her son? 'You are everything to us, our only comfort, our only hope.' Oh, Mother!"
His bitterness grew stronger with every moment. If he had happened to meet Mr. Luzhin just then, he might have killed him.

"Hmm... yes, that's true," he went on, chasing one feverish thought after another. "It's true that 'it takes time and care to know a person,' but there's no mystery about Mr. Luzhin. The main thing is he's 'a practical man and _seems_ kind' -- what a feat, arranging shipment of their bags and trunk! A kind man, obviously! But his _bride_ and her mother are supposed to ride in a peasant cart with a tarp over it. I know those carts -- I've ridden in one. Never mind! It's only ninety versts, and then they can 'travel quite comfortably in third class' for a thousand versts! Quite right. You have to live within your means. But what about you, Mr. Luzhin? She's your bride.... And you must realize that her mother has to borrow against her pension just to make the trip. Sure, it's a business arrangement -- a partnership with equal shares and shared expenses; meals included, but bring your own tobacco. The businessman has gotten the better of them here, too. The luggage will cost less than their fares and probably ship for free. How do neither of them see this? Or do they just not want to? And they're pleased, pleased! And to think this is just the beginning -- the real fruits are yet to come! But what really matters isn't the cheapness, isn't the stinginess -- it's the _tone_ of the whole thing. Because this will be the tone after the marriage. It's a preview. And Mother -- why should she spend so freely? What will she have left by the time she reaches Petersburg? Three silver rubles or two 'paper ones,' as _she_ says... that old woman... hmm. What does she plan to live on in Petersburg afterward? She already has reason to suspect she _won't_ be able to live with Dunya after the wedding, not even for the first few months. The good man has no doubt dropped a hint about that too, though mother would deny it: 'I shall refuse,' she says. So who is she counting on? On what's left of her hundred-and-twenty-ruble pension after Afanasy Ivanovich's debt is paid? She knits woolen shawls and embroiders cuffs, ruining her old eyes. And all her shawls add at most twenty rubles a year to her hundred and twenty -- I know that. So she's pinning all her hopes on Mr. Luzhin's generosity: 'He'll offer it himself, he'll insist.' You may wait a long time for that! That's how it always is with these Schilleresque noble souls: up to the very last moment every goose is a swan, up to the last moment they hope for the best and refuse to see anything wrong. And though they have an inkling of the truth, they won't face it until it's forced on them. The very thought makes them shudder. They push the truth away with both hands until the man they've dressed up in borrowed colors puts a fool's cap on them personally. I wonder if Mr. Luzhin has any medals. I bet he has the Order of St. Anna in his buttonhole and wears it to dinners with merchants and contractors. He'll certainly wear it at his wedding! To hell with him, enough.

"Well... Mother I can understand -- God bless her, that's how she is. But Dunya? Dunya, darling, as if I don't know you! You were almost twenty when I last saw you, and I understood you even then. Mother writes that 'Dunya can put up with a great deal.' I know that very well. I've known it for two and a half years, and for two and a half years I've been thinking about exactly that -- that 'Dunya can put up with a great deal.' If she could put up with Mr. Svidrigailov and everything else, she can certainly put up with a great deal. And now mother and she have decided she can also put up with Mr. Luzhin, who expounds his theory that wives rescued from destitution should be forever grateful to their husbands -- and expounds it practically on the first meeting. Granted, he 'let it slip,' though he's supposed to be a sensible man (or maybe it wasn't a slip at all -- maybe he wanted to make his position clear from the start). But Dunya -- Dunya? She sees through the man, of course, but she'll have to live with him. She'd live on black bread and water before she'd sell her soul. She wouldn't trade her moral freedom for comfort. She wouldn't trade it for all of Schleswig-Holstein, let alone Mr. Luzhin's money. No, Dunya was never that sort when I knew her, and... she's still the same, of course! Yes, there's no denying the Svidrigailovs are hard to swallow. Spending your life as a governess in the provinces for two hundred rubles a year is bitter. But I know she'd rather be a slave on a plantation or a serf under a German master than degrade her soul and her moral dignity by binding herself forever to a man she doesn't respect and has nothing in common with -- all for her own advantage. Even if Mr. Luzhin were made of pure gold or were one enormous diamond, she would never have agreed to become his legal concubine. So why is she agreeing? What's the point? What's the answer? It's obvious: for herself, for her own comfort, to save her own life -- she would never sell herself. But for someone else, she'll do it! For someone she loves, someone she adores, she'll sell herself! That's what it comes down to. For her brother, for her mother, she'll sell herself! She'll sell everything! In situations like this, 'we overcome our moral feelings when necessary' -- freedom, peace, conscience, everything gets brought to market. Let my life be ruined, as long as my loved ones are happy! More than that, we become rationalizers, we learn to be Jesuitical, and for a while we can even soothe ourselves, convince ourselves it's our duty for a good cause. That's exactly what's happening here, clear as day. Rodion Romanovich Raskolnikov is obviously the central figure in this whole business. Oh yes, she can secure his happiness, keep him at the university, make him a partner in the firm, guarantee his entire future. Maybe he'll even become a rich man someday -- prosperous, respected, perhaps even end his life as a famous man! But what about Mother? It's all about Rodya, precious Rodya, her firstborn! For such a son, who wouldn't sacrifice such a daughter! Oh, loving, biased hearts! Why stop there? For his sake we wouldn't even shrink from Sonya's fate -- Sonya, Sonya Marmeladov, the eternal victim, as long as the world exists. Have you both measured your sacrifice? Really measured it? Is it right? Can you bear it? Is it worth it? Is there any sense in it? Let me tell you, Dunya: Sonya's life is no worse than life with Mr. Luzhin. 'There can be no question of love,' mother writes. But what if there's no question of respect either? What if instead there's only revulsion, contempt, disgust -- what then? So you'll have to 'keep up appearances' too. Do you understand what that means? Do you understand that the Luzhin kind of smartness is exactly the same as Sonya's -- maybe worse, more vile, more degrading -- because in your case, Dunya, it's a bargain for luxuries, while for Sonya it's literally a matter of starvation? It has to be paid for, Dunya, this kind of smartness. And what if later it proves more than you can bear, and you regret it? The bitterness, the misery, the curses, the tears hidden from the whole world -- because you're not Marfa Petrovna! And how will Mother feel then? Even now she's uneasy, worried -- but when she sees it all clearly? And me? What exactly do you take me for? I won't accept your sacrifice, Dunya! I won't accept it, Mother! It will not happen as long as I'm alive! It will not! I refuse!"
He suddenly stopped and stood still.

"It will not happen? But what are you going to do to stop it? Forbid it? And what right do you have? What can you promise them in return that would give you such a right? To devote your whole life to them _after you finish your studies and get a position_? Sure, we've heard that before -- those are just _words_. But what about now? Now something has to be done, right now -- do you understand? And what are you doing now? You're living off them. They borrow against their hundred-ruble pension. They borrow from the Svidrigailovs. How are you going to save them from the Svidrigailovs, from Afanasy Ivanovich Vakhrushin, you future millionaire Zeus who would arrange their lives? In another ten years? In ten years, mother will be blind from knitting shawls -- maybe from crying, too. She'll be worn to a shadow from going hungry. And my sister? Just imagine what might have become of your sister in ten years. What could happen to her in those ten years? Can you picture it?"

He tormented himself with these questions and even found a kind of perverse pleasure in it. None of these questions were new or sudden -- they were old, familiar wounds. It had been a long time since they first started to grip and tear at his heart. Long ago his current anguish had begun. It had grown and gathered strength, ripened and concentrated, until it took the shape of a terrifying, frenzied, fantastic question that gnawed at his heart and mind, demanding an answer. Now his mother's letter had struck like a thunderbolt. It was clear that he could no longer sit passively agonizing over unanswered questions. He had to do something -- do it now, do it fast. He had to make a decision, or else...
"Or give up on life altogether!" he cried suddenly, in a frenzy. "Accept your fate meekly, once and for all, and suffocate everything inside you, giving up every claim to action, to life, to love!"

"Do you understand, sir, do you understand what it means when you have absolutely nowhere to turn?" Marmeladov's question suddenly surfaced in his mind. "For every man must have somewhere to turn...."

He started. Another thought -- one he'd had yesterday -- slipped back into his mind. But he didn't start because the thought was returning. He had known, had _felt in advance_, that it would come back. He'd been waiting for it. Besides, it was not just yesterday's thought. The difference was that a month ago, even yesterday, it had been a mere dream. But now... now it appeared as something other than a dream entirely -- it had taken on a new, menacing, completely unfamiliar form, and he suddenly became aware of this.... His head was pounding, and a darkness fell before his eyes.

He looked around urgently, searching for something. He needed to sit down and was looking for a bench. He was walking along K----- Boulevard. There was a bench about a hundred paces ahead. He walked toward it as fast as he could, but on the way he ran into a small incident that absorbed all his attention. While searching for the bench, he had noticed a woman walking about twenty paces ahead, but at first he paid her no more attention than anything else that crossed his path. He had often gone home without noticing his route and was used to walking that way. But there was something so immediately strange about this woman that gradually his attention was drawn to her -- at first reluctantly, almost resentfully, and then more and more intently. He suddenly wanted to understand what was so strange about her. To begin with, she appeared to be very young, and she was walking in the blazing heat bareheaded, without a parasol or gloves, waving her arms in an absurd way. She wore a dress of some thin silky material, but it was put on crookedly, barely fastened, torn open near the waist with a large piece hanging loose. A small scarf was draped around her bare throat but sat crooked, slipping to one side. The girl was also walking unsteadily, stumbling and staggering. She finally captured Raskolnikov's full attention. He caught up with her at the bench, and when she reached it, she collapsed onto it in the corner, let her head fall back, and closed her eyes, apparently in total exhaustion. Looking at her closely, he saw at once that she was completely drunk. It was a strange and disturbing sight. He could barely believe he wasn't mistaken. Before him was the face of a very young girl -- fair-haired, sixteen at most, possibly only fifteen -- a pretty little face, but flushed, heavy-looking, almost swollen. The girl seemed barely aware of what she was doing. She crossed one leg over the other in an indecent way, showing every sign of being oblivious to the fact that she was on a public street.

Raskolnikov didn't sit down, but he couldn't bring himself to leave her, and stood there facing her in confusion. This boulevard was never very busy, and now at two in the afternoon, in the crushing heat, it was completely deserted. Yet on the far side of the boulevard, about fifteen paces away, a gentleman stood at the edge of the sidewalk. He, too, clearly wanted to approach the girl for his own purposes. He, too, had probably noticed her from a distance and followed her, only to find Raskolnikov in his way. He glared at Raskolnikov, though he tried not to be noticed, and waited impatiently for the unwelcome stranger in rags to move on. His intentions were obvious. The gentleman was a plump, stocky man of about thirty, fashionably dressed, with a ruddy complexion, red lips, and a mustache. Raskolnikov was seized with fury -- a sudden urge to insult this fat dandy somehow. He left the girl for a moment and walked toward the man.
"Hey! You, Svidrigailov! What do you want here?" he shouted, clenching his fists and laughing, sputtering with rage.
"What do you mean?" the man asked sternly, scowling with haughty surprise.
"Get away from here. That's what I mean."
"How dare you, you filthy tramp!"

He raised his cane. Raskolnikov lunged at him with his fists, without stopping to consider that this heavyset gentleman was easily a match for two men his size. But at that instant someone grabbed him from behind, and a policeman stepped between them.
"Enough, gentlemen. No fighting in a public place, please. Who are you? What do you want?" he asked Raskolnikov sternly, taking note of his rags.
Raskolnikov studied him closely. He had an honest, sensible, military face with gray mustache and sideburns.

"You're exactly who I need," Raskolnikov cried, grabbing his arm. "I'm a student -- Raskolnikov.... You may as well know that too," he added, turning to the gentleman. "Come with me, I have something to show you."
Taking the policeman by the hand, he led him toward the bench.

"Look -- she's completely drunk. She just came down the boulevard. There's no telling who she is or where she comes from, but she doesn't look like a professional. More likely someone got her drunk and took advantage of her... for the first time... do you follow? And then they put her out on the street like this. Look at how her dress is torn, look at how it was put on. She didn't dress herself -- it was done by someone else, by clumsy hands, a man's hands. That's obvious. Now look over there: that man I was about to fight -- I don't know him, never seen him before -- but he spotted her on the road too, drunk, not knowing what she's doing, and now he's very eager to get his hands on her, to take her somewhere while she's in this state. That's certain, believe me. I saw him watching her, following her, but I got in his way, and now he's just waiting for me to leave. See, he's moved off a bit, pretending to roll a cigarette.... Think about how we can keep her away from him and get her home."

The policeman grasped the situation immediately. The fat gentleman was easy enough to figure out. He turned to examine the girl, bending down for a closer look, and his face showed genuine compassion.

"What a shame!" he said, shaking his head. "She's just a child! She's been tricked -- you can see that at a glance. Listen, miss," he said, addressing her, "where do you live?" The girl opened her weary, glazed eyes, stared blankly at him, and waved her hand.
"Here," said Raskolnikov, reaching into his pocket and finding twenty kopecks. "Take this, call a cab, and have him drive her to her address. If only we could find out where she lives!"
"Miss! Miss!" the policeman began again, taking the money. "I'll get you a cab and take you home myself. Where should I take you? Where do you live?"
"Go away! Leave me alone," the girl mumbled, waving her hand again.
"Oh dear, oh dear! What a disgrace, miss, what a shame!" He shook his head again -- shocked, sympathetic, outraged.
"This is a tricky one," the policeman said to Raskolnikov, giving him another quick once-over. He, too, must have thought Raskolnikov a strange sight -- dressed in rags and handing over money!
"Did you run into her far from here?" he asked.
"I'm telling you, she was walking ahead of me, staggering, right here on the boulevard. She barely made it to the bench before she collapsed."

"The disgraceful things that happen in this world, God have mercy! An innocent creature like this, already drunk! She's been tricked, no doubt about it. Look at how her dress is torn.... The depravity you see nowadays! And she probably comes from a decent family too, maybe poor.... There are plenty like that these days. She looks refined, almost like a lady." And he bent over her again.
Perhaps he had daughters of his own growing up like that -- "looking like ladies, refined," with pretensions to respectability and elegance....
"The main thing," Raskolnikov insisted, "is to keep her out of that scoundrel's hands! Why should she be violated? It's perfectly clear what he wants. Look at the brute -- he's not leaving!"

Raskolnikov spoke loudly and pointed at him. The man heard and seemed about to lose his temper again, but thought better of it and contented himself with a contemptuous look. Then he walked slowly another ten paces away and stopped again.
"We can keep her from him," the policeman said thoughtfully, "if only she'd tell us where to take her. Miss! Hey, miss!" He bent over her once more.

She suddenly opened her eyes wide, looked at him with something like comprehension, got up from the bench, and started walking back the way she had come. "Disgusting people -- they won't leave me alone!" she said, waving her hand again. She walked quickly, though still staggering. The dandy followed her along a different path, keeping his eyes on her.
"Don't worry, I won't let him get to her," the policeman said firmly, and set off after them.
"The depravity you see nowadays!" he repeated aloud with a sigh.
At that moment something seemed to sting Raskolnikov. In an instant, his feelings reversed completely.
"Hey! Wait!" he shouted after the policeman.
The officer turned around.
"Forget it! What's it to you? Let her go! Let him have his fun." He pointed at the dandy. "What business is it of yours?"
The policeman stared at him, bewildered. Raskolnikov laughed.
"Well!" the policeman said with a contemptuous wave, and walked off after the dandy and the girl, probably thinking Raskolnikov was a madman or something worse.

"He took my twenty kopecks," Raskolnikov muttered angrily once he was alone. "Well, let him squeeze some money out of the other one too, for letting him have the girl, and be done with it. Why did I have to interfere? Is it my place to help? Do I have any right to help? Let them eat each other alive -- what's it to me? And how dare I give away twenty kopecks? Were they even mine?"

Despite those strange words, he felt deeply miserable. He sat down on the empty bench. His thoughts drifted aimlessly.... He couldn't fix his mind on anything. He wanted to forget himself entirely, forget everything, and then wake up and start life over....

"Poor girl!" he said, looking at the empty corner where she had sat. "She'll come to her senses and cry, and then her mother will find out.... She'll beat her -- a horrible, shameful beating -- and maybe throw her out. And even if she doesn't, the Darya Frantsovnas will catch wind of it, and the girl will soon be slipping out on the sly here and there. Then the hospital will follow (that's always the fate of those girls from decent families who go wrong on the sly), and then... the hospital again... vodka... taverns... more hospital. In two or three years -- a wreck, dead at eighteen or nineteen.... Haven't I seen cases like that? Every single one of them ended up that way. Ugh! But so what? That's how it should be, they tell us. A certain percentage, they say, has to go that way every year... to the devil, presumably, so the rest can stay pure and unbothered. A percentage! What wonderful words they have -- so scientific, so reassuring.... Once you've said 'percentage,' there's nothing more to worry about. If we used a different word... maybe we'd feel more uneasy.... But what if Dunya ends up as one of the percentage? Part of one, if not another?

"But where am I going?" he thought suddenly. "Strange. I came out for a reason. As soon as I read the letter I rushed out.... I was heading to Vasilyevsky Island, to Razumikhin's. That's right... now I remember. But why? What put the idea of going to Razumikhin into my head just now? That's odd."

He marveled at himself. Razumikhin was one of his old university friends. The remarkable thing was that Raskolnikov had virtually no friends at the university. He kept to himself, saw no one, and didn't welcome visitors -- and soon everyone stopped trying. He took no part in student gatherings, discussions, or amusements. He studied with fierce intensity, sparing himself nothing, and was respected for it, but nobody liked him. He was very poor, and there was something haughty and secretive about him, as though he were hiding something. Some of his classmates felt he looked down on them all like children, as if he were superior in intellect, knowledge, and convictions, as if their interests and beliefs were beneath him.

With Razumikhin, though, he had gotten along -- or at least he was more open and communicative with him than with anyone else. It was impossible not to get along with Razumikhin. He was an exceptionally good-natured and straightforward young man, kindhearted to the point of simplicity, though both depth and dignity lay hidden beneath that simplicity. His better friends understood this, and everyone was fond of him. He was very intelligent, though he could be quite naive at times. He was striking to look at -- tall, thin, black-haired, and always badly shaved. He could be boisterous, and he was reputed to have enormous physical strength. One night, while out celebrating, he had floored a gigantic policeman with a single punch. His capacity for drinking was limitless, but he could also abstain completely. He sometimes went too far with his pranks but was equally capable of doing without them. Another remarkable thing about Razumikhin: no setback discouraged him, and no hardship seemed able to crush him. He could live anywhere and endure extreme cold and hunger. He was very poor, supporting himself entirely by whatever odd jobs he could find. He had endless ways of earning money. He once went an entire winter without heating his room, and claimed he preferred it because you sleep better in the cold. For now, he too had been forced to leave the university, but only temporarily -- he was working with all his might to save enough to go back. Raskolnikov hadn't seen him in four months, and Razumikhin didn't even know his address. About two months ago they had passed each other on the street, but Raskolnikov had turned away and even crossed to the other side to avoid being noticed. Razumikhin had seen him but walked on by, not wanting to bother him.
